title: How to Handle Secrets in Helm
content_md: TL;DR Base64 encoding is not encryption : Kubernetes Secrets are base64 encoded, not encrypted, so committing one to a Helm chart puts a working credential in Git. Encrypt in the chart or sync at deploy time : Encrypt values inside the chart with helm-secrets and SOPS or Sealed Secrets, or keep values out of the chart and sync them at deploy time with External Secrets Operator or Vault Secrets Operator. External Secrets Operator as the default pick : External Secrets Operator needs nothing installed where Helm runs, so Argo CD, Flux, and GitHub Actions work unchanged, which makes it the default choice. SOPS with age instead of PGP keys : Use age encryption instead of PGP keys with SOPS. It gives comparable protection for encrypting a values file, with far simpler key management. Reloader for pods after secret rotation : Rotating a secret does not restart your pods, a gap most guides miss. Add Reloader and the auto annotation to close the gap. If you have ever pasted a database password into values.yaml and then paused for a second before running git commit , this one is for you. A Helm chart is built to be shared. A password is built to be shared with nobody. This guide walks through the four ways teams reconcile those two facts, with a working example for each, plus the rotation gap that tends to show up months later.
